task: correct and finish a photograph in a photo editor (Lightroom, Lightroom Mobile, Snapseed, Photoshop Camera Raw, Apple Photos, Capture One): open a real source photo, judge what is wrong with it, then work the corrections — exposure and contrast, white balance, crop and straighten, highlight and shadow recovery, spot or blemish removal, and local adjustments brushed or masked onto part of the frame — checking the result against the original as you go, and export or save at a chosen size and format; complete when the export/save dialog is confirmed or the finished image is written out. Surface pinned: the editing session on one photograph — the arc is CORRECTIVE, taking an existing image from flawed to finished. Off-task: building a composite or a layout from multiple images (that is graphic design), generating or extending an image with AI, applying a purchased preset with no further judgement, gear and camera reviews, before/after showcases with no visible editing, and shooting tutorials that never reach an editor.

tree.label: Correct and finish a photograph
tree.note: 1 to get the photo into the editor - 1.4 when the photo arrives already edited, 1.7 only in oiAO, 1.9 whenever a price or a paid feature appears. 2 before the first slider, and again before 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 - the person names the flaw, then fixes it. 3 first when the person needs to crop the photo before placing the masks (QTuO, 29mt), and later or not at all elsewhere. then 4, then 5; after 5, the person may need to repeat 4 if the colour adjustments change the light (oiAO, OSj7). 6 for each region that needs its own fix - after 5 in the Lightroom videos, before 5 in Ao-f, and in Snapseed by painting a global edit onto part of the frame. 7 after 6, or before it where the presenter makes the finishing adjustments to the whole photo first. 8 after every one of 3 to 7 and again at the end. 9 when the person is done - they confirm the edit at 9.1 in nine videos, export the photo through 9.2 to 9.6 in five, and apply the edit to other photos at 9.8.

children.label: Open the photo
children.note: 1.1 in every video - through 1.2 first in OXgO. then 1.3. 1.4 where the photo arrives with edits on it. 1.5 in the Photoshop videos before any correction. 1.6 where the person picks a rendering before the sliders. 1.7 only in oiAO. 1.8 mid-task, when a tool in the first editor cannot do the job or the person needs the raw photo in Photoshop. 1.9 whenever a price, a paid tier or a promo appears, at any step.

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to visually gauge the image and subjectively balance the vignette's intensity for a natural result.
questions.verify_form: The agent reduced the vignette's opacity - check it is not too strong.
questions.check: What opacity value does the page show on the Levels layer?
questions.say_example: The Levels layer's opacity dropped to <60>.

questions.question: Is the slider that moved the one that was named?
questions.why: The audio instructed changing the roughness to 35, but the screen showed the size slider being adjusted to 35 instead.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the intended visual effect because the agent mistakenly changed the brush size instead of its roughness.
questions.check: Does the slider that actually moved match the slider named out loud - Roughness versus Size?
questions.say_example: The narration named Roughness, but the slider that actually moved to <35> is Size.

children.label: Compare against the original
children.note: 8.1 after every one of 3 to 7 in most videos and again at the end. 8.2 inside 5 and 6 - once per panel or per mask, before the next. 8.3 where the editor keeps a stack. 8.4 for sharpening and noise. 8.5 whenever 8.1 or 8.2 says the last step made it worse. 8.6 near the end in the long videos, and it sends the person back into 4, 5 or 6. in this goal the person decides whether the problem named in 2.4 is fixed.

questions.question: Were the features named at the start actually used later on?
questions.why: The initial promise at 0:14 to showcase new updates is fulfilled when the screen later shows the active application of Smart Adjustments and Dust Removal.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the guarantee that the agent will follow through on specific thematic goals or tool explorations set at the beginning of the editing session.
questions.check: Does the page later show the features named at the start (for example <Smart Adjustments and Dust Removal>) actually applied?
questions.say_example: <Smart Adjustments and Dust Removal> were named at the start, but neither shows as applied anywhere later.

children.label: Toggle the whole edit against the original

questions.question: Is the before/after split screen currently active in the workspace?
questions.why: A sighted user instantly sees if the workspace is split in half, but a delegated agent might leave the view in comparison mode, making it confusing to evaluate the final full-screen result.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to know if they are looking at the final edited image or a split comparison that obscures half the frame.
questions.check: Does the page show the before/after split-screen view still active in the workspace?
questions.say_example: The workspace is still split into Before/After view.

questions.question: Does toggling between Before and After show a visible difference, or do the two look the same?
questions.why: Toggling the 'Before' view allows you to verify that the accumulated adjustments have genuinely improved the image without over-editing.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the subjective ability to judge whether the subtle, accumulated corrections align with your personal aesthetic vision for the photograph.
questions.check: When toggled between Before and After, does the preview show any visible change, or does it look identical?
questions.say_example: Toggling Before and After shows no difference. The edit may have landed on the wrong photo or version.

questions.question: What adjustments are still needed to match your target edit?
questions.why: Toggling between the current state and the target image reveals subtle differences in color and contrast that dictate your final tweaks.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to train your own eye to spot nuanced differences in contrast and color grading.
questions.check: Toggling between the current edit and the target reference image, are there visible differences in color or contrast?
questions.say_example: Toggled against the target, <the shadows> still read darker than the reference.

questions.question: Does the finishing before/after comparison show a visible overall change from the original?
questions.why: Comparing the finished image to the initial dull raw file confirms that the intended transformation was successfully achieved.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means you lose the ability to personally verify that your specific creative vision for the photo was realized.
questions.check: At the finishing before/after toggle, does the comparison show a visible overall change from the original?
questions.say_example: Before and after, the photo went from <flat and underexposed> to <brighter, with the colour cast corrected>.

questions.question: Does toggling this adjustment's checkmark show a visible change in the preview?
questions.why: Toggling the blue checkmark next to a setting like White Balance lets you isolate and evaluate the exact difference that single correction made.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to apply your own visual judgment to verify whether an individual tweak truly enhanced the photograph.
questions.check: Does toggling this adjustment's checkmark off and on show a visible change in the preview?
questions.say_example: Toggling the White Balance checkmark off and on shows no visible change. It may not be doing anything.

questions.question: Does toggling this mask actually lighten the dark corner?
questions.why: Toggling the mask's eye icon lets you visually verify that the local adjustment effectively removed the dark corner.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the subjective visual judgment of whether the local adjustment seamlessly fixed the background distraction without looking unnatural.
questions.check: Toggling the mask's eye icon, does the dark corner distraction actually lighten, or does the corner look unchanged?
questions.say_example: Toggling the mask off and on, <the dark corner> looks the same either way.

questions.question: With the skin mask on, is there still pore texture, or has the skin gone waxy?
questions.why: Toggling the mask on and off lets you visually confirm that the skin texture remains realistic rather than overly blurred.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the subjective, aesthetic judgment of deciding exactly how much skin texture should be preserved in the portrait.
questions.check: Toggling the skin mask off and on, does the zoomed-in skin still show pore and texture detail, or has it gone smooth and waxy?
questions.say_example: Toggled on, <the cheek> has gone smooth and waxy. There's no pore texture left.

questions.question: Toggling each mask off and on, does the photo actually change?
questions.why: Toggling the eye icons in the Masks panel isolates the visual impact of each local adjustment on the subject's face.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the direct visual understanding of how specific local corrections address individual flaws like shiny skin or a reddish nose.
questions.check: When each mask's eye icon is toggled off and on, does the preview visibly change?
questions.say_example: Toggling <the sunglasses mask>, nothing in the preview changes. It may be pointed at the wrong area.

questions.question: Which edit layers should you toggle to review the progression of your adjustments?
questions.why: Stepping through the edit stack from the original photo to the final brush strokes lets you verify that each adjustment actually improved the image.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to visually evaluate the step-by-step progression and decide if any specific layer needs to be dialed back.
questions.verify_form: The agent toggled layers to review progression - check which layers.
questions.check: Which layers does the page show toggled in sequence, from original to final?
questions.say_example: Reviewed layers in order, <Basic, Color, three brush masks>

questions.question: Which specific areas did you target with mask adjustments to finish the image?
questions.why: Toggling the visibility icon next to each mask in the panel reveals exactly how the sky, subject highlights, and sunglasses were individually altered.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the visual confirmation that each local adjustment perfectly targets its intended area without unwanted spillover into the rest of the image.
questions.check: Which areas does the Masks panel list as targeted?
questions.say_example: Masked <the sky, the subject's highlights and the sunglasses>

children.label: Zoom in to check the detail

questions.question: Should you zoom in to ensure your brush mask is precise?
questions.why: Zooming in while brushing out an effect allows you to make a precise selection and avoid accidentally removing the effect from adjacent areas.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the tactile precision of zooming in to perfectly trace complex edges, risking a sloppy mask that spills over into unintended areas.
questions.verify_form: The agent zoomed in to brush, or did not - check the mask edges.
questions.check: Is the zoom level at 100% or higher while the brush mask is being painted?
questions.say_example: The brush is being painted at <fit-to-screen> zoom, not 100%. Edges may land imprecisely.

questions.question: Should you zoom in to check the effect of the noise reduction?
questions.why: Using the top-left slider to zoom in to 100% allows you to see exactly how the noise reduction affects fine details at the pixel level.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to visually confirm that the image retains your preferred balance of sharpness and detail after the noise reduction is applied.
questions.check: Is the zoom level shown at 100% (1:1) when reviewing the noise reduction?
questions.say_example: Noise reduction is being reviewed at <fit-to-screen>, not 100%. Grain and smearing won't show clearly.

questions.question: Has the heavy editing introduced color banding or posterization in the smooth gradients?
questions.why: Pushing contrast and saturation too far, especially on compressed files, causes smooth areas like skies to break apart into ugly, visible bands of color that ruin the image.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the critical quality control check of zooming in to ensure the edits haven't mathematically destroyed the image's smooth transitions.
questions.check: At 100% zoom, does a smooth gradient area, like the sky, show visible banding or blocky posterization?
questions.say_example: At 100% zoom, <the sky's gradient> shows visible banding in horizontal bands.

questions.question: What zoom is the noise reduction being checked at?
questions.why: The interface displays the exact zoom level (e.g., 100% or 1:1), which is critical because noise and sharpening artifacts cannot be accurately evaluated if the image is scaled to fit the screen.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user cannot visually verify that the agent is actually reviewing the pixels at a 1:1 ratio, meaning any claims about sharpness or noise might be based on a flawed, compressed preview.
questions.check: What zoom percentage does the interface display while noise reduction is being reviewed?
questions.say_example: Checked the noise reduction at <66%> zoom

children.label: Undo, reset or revert a step

questions.question: Should you reset the light adjustments to start over?
questions.why: Clicking the reset arrow next to the Light panel clears all previous exposure adjustments so you can establish a fresh baseline.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative freedom to scrap an initial attempt and iteratively dial in the perfect exposure baseline yourself.
questions.verify_form: The agent reset the Light group - check that every sub-slider went back to zero and that the reset was meant, not a stray click.
questions.check: After the reset, do all of the Light group's sliders show zero?
questions.say_example: The Light group's sliders all just reset to zero. Was that the plan, or a stray click on the reset arrow?

questions.question: Should you undo your spot removal attempts if the tool fails to cleanly erase the object?
questions.why: When the native healing tool struggles with complex objects and leaves messy artifacts, undoing the changes prevents destructive edits and signals that a more advanced pixel editor is needed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to recognize the limitations of the current tool and the judgment to revert bad edits before moving to a more capable application.
questions.verify_form: The agent undid a failed removal, or left it - check for artifacts.
questions.check: Does the removal preview show a messy artifact or repeated pattern where the object was removed?
questions.say_example: The removal over <the sign> left a visible smear. The undo hasn't been used yet.

questions.question: Is this new graduated filter in the right place, with the right settings?
questions.why: If a graduated filter is dragged at the wrong angle or applies unwanted settings left over from a previous edit, undoing it immediately is faster than trying to manually reset all the sliders and reposition the lines.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the efficiency of quickly scrapping a bad mask placement to start fresh, potentially leading to a messy, over-corrected sky.
questions.verify_form: The agent undid a misplaced gradient, or left it - check the sky.
questions.check: Does the graduated filter's angle or carried-over settings match the intended edit, or do they look left over from a previous mask?
questions.say_example: The new graduated filter carried over <a strong warm tint> from the previous mask, at an angle that cuts across the horizon.

questions.question: Should you revert the edits made to the photo?
questions.why: The screen displays a 'Revert' option, allowing the user to discard all changes if the edits are unsatisfactory.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the subjective choice of whether to keep the current edits or discard them to start over.
questions.verify_form: The agent reverted the edits or kept them - check which; Revert throws away every adjustment in the session.
questions.check: Does the page show a Revert option that would discard every edit made in this session?
questions.say_example: Revert would throw away every edit made this session, the crop, the masks, all of it. Keep going, or actually revert?

children.label: Re-walk the edit with fresh eyes

questions.question: Do the two passes on the same slider add up to what was wanted?
questions.why: Across two separate Tune Image adjustments, the Shadows parameter was first increased to +47 and later decreased to -4, resulting in a net change of +43.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to iteratively fine-tune a specific parameter based on how the image evolves during the editing process.
questions.check: Do the two separate Shadows adjustments, first raised then lowered, net to a value consistent with the intended look?
questions.say_example: Shadows went up to <+47> in one pass and down to <-4> in another. The slider now reads <-4>, which isn't what the first pass was after.

questions.question: Do you need to readjust the shadows setting after changing other exposure parameters?
questions.why: Changing other settings can alter the overall contrast, requiring you to dial the shadows slider back to a value like 86 to keep the image looking natural.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the subjective visual judgment required to balance shadow recovery perfectly against other interacting exposure edits.
questions.verify_form: The agent readjusted the shadows after other sliders - check the final value looks natural.
questions.check: What value does the Shadows slider read after the other exposure sliders were changed?
questions.say_example: Shadows settled at <86> after the other exposure sliders moved.

questions.question: Do you need to refine the overall exposure and highlights before applying local masks?
questions.why: Adjusting the global exposure and highlights establishes a balanced baseline for the entire image before isolating specific areas.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally judge the foundational brightness and contrast that sets the mood for your final image.
questions.verify_form: The agent refined exposure and highlights before the masks - check the baseline.
questions.check: What do the global Exposure and Highlights sliders read before any local masks are added?
questions.say_example: Global Exposure sits at <+0.3> and Highlights at <-20> before the masks go on.

questions.question: Should you fine-tune the global exposure and tint after applying your color grading?
questions.why: Applying color grading often shifts the image's overall brightness and color cast, requiring a return to the Basic panel sliders to restore balance.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to make subjective, aesthetic micro-adjustments to the image's lighting and color balance.
questions.verify_form: The agent fine-tuned exposure and tint after the grade - check the balance came back.
questions.check: What do the global Exposure and Tint sliders read after color grading was applied?
questions.say_example: After grading, global Exposure moved to <-0.2> and Tint to <+5> to restore balance.

questions.question: How should you balance the extreme highlights and shadows?
questions.why: Iteratively adjusting the white and black sliders establishes the image's true tonal range and prevents clipping in the brightest and darkest areas.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative control of visually going back and forth with the sliders until the contrast feels exactly right for your aesthetic.
questions.verify_form: The agent went back and forth on whites and blacks - check the final range does not clip.
questions.check: What do the Whites and Blacks sliders read, and does the histogram show clipping at either end?
questions.say_example: Whites sit at <+30> and Blacks at <-35>. No clipping shows at either end of the histogram.

questions.question: Are the masked areas too bright?
questions.why: Decreasing the exposure on the masked edges ensures those specific areas do not look unnaturally bright compared to the rest of the image.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the subtle, subjective judgment of exactly how bright those specific masked regions should be to balance the overall composition.
questions.check: What exposure value do the masked edges read after the adjustment?
questions.say_example: The masked edges' exposure dropped to <-0.4>.

questions.question: Which global adjustments should you fine-tune after reviewing the whole image?
questions.why: Revisiting the contrast and specific color channels like green saturation and blue luminance ensures the final image looks balanced and natural.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to apply your personal aesthetic taste to the final color balance and contrast of the photograph.
questions.verify_form: The agent fine-tuned global adjustments - check contrast and colours.
questions.check: What do the global Contrast and the green and blue channel values read?
questions.say_example: Global contrast moved to <+10>, green saturation to <-8>, blue luminance to <+5>.

questions.question: Do the colors still look natural with fresh eyes, or do specific hues need dialing back?
questions.why: Stepping away and returning to the image preview reveals if certain colors, like the aquas and greens, have become overly vibrant during the editing process.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the human ability to reset your visual perception and intuitively judge if the overall color balance feels authentic.
questions.check: Do the aqua and green HSL saturation values read unusually high compared to the rest of the palette?
questions.say_example: Aqua saturation sits at <+40> and green at <+35>. Both well above the other hues.

questions.question: What final adjustments do you need to make after reviewing the image with fresh eyes?
questions.why: Reviewing the image after a break reveals subtle imbalances, showing that the overall exposure needs dialing back while specific colors like aqua require a slight boost.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the subjective aesthetic judgment that comes from reviewing a nearly finished image with fresh eyes to make subtle, personalized color tweaks.
questions.verify_form: The agent made final tweaks with fresh eyes - check exposure and aqua.
questions.check: What do global Exposure and aqua saturation read after the final review pass?
questions.say_example: Global exposure dropped slightly to <-0.15> and aqua saturation eased back to <+20>.

questions.question: How much should you reduce the global highlights to balance the image after your local adjustments?
questions.why: Significantly reducing the highlights in the Basic panel ensures the brightest parts of the image retain detail without clashing with the new local edits.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the visual judgment required to perfectly balance the overall exposure against the specific areas you just retouched.
questions.verify_form: The agent reduced global highlights after the masks - check the detail.
questions.check: What does the global Highlights slider read after the local masks were added?
questions.say_example: Global Highlights dropped to <-45> after the masks went on.

children.label: Save the result
children.note: 9.1 closes a tool in Snapseed and Camera Raw and closes the edit in Photos and Lightroom Mobile - it is the task's end in nine videos. 9.2 where the person exports: then 9.3, 9.4 and 9.5 in the dialog, in the order it lists them, and 9.6 after the click. 9.8 where the edit is carried to other photos - before 9.2 in _8_p and NFrz, instead of it in OXgO's style step. fifteen videos never reach 9.2.

children.label: Commit the edit in the editor

questions.question: Are these tuning values ready to apply?
questions.why: The bottom bar displays a checkmark and an 'X', requiring a decision to either commit the current edits to the image or discard them.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally evaluate whether these specific adjustments actually improve the photo before committing them.
questions.verify_form: The agent applied the Tune Image edits - check the sliders it committed before the checkmark.
questions.check: What slider values does the page show about to be committed with the checkmark?
questions.say_example: Tune Image is about to apply with <shadows +47, highlights -20, temp +8>.

questions.question: Should you apply the current sharpening setting?
questions.why: The screen displayed a sharpening value of 0 with options to confirm or cancel, requiring a choice on whether to apply the adjustment.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide exactly how much sharpening the image needs to look its best.
questions.check: What sharpening value does the page show set to 0 before the confirm or cancel choice?
questions.say_example: Sharpening reads <0> at the confirm step. Nothing would actually change if applied.

questions.question: Is this the curve to commit?
questions.why: Tapping the checkmark applies the specific tonal and contrast changes made in the curves interface to the overall image.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative control of deciding exactly how moody or contrasted the image should feel based on your personal aesthetic.
questions.check: What shape or points does the curve show before the checkmark commits it?
questions.say_example: The curve shows an S-shape lifting <the midtones> before committing.

questions.question: Do these selective edits look right before you apply them?
questions.why: Confirming the selective tool applies the targeted changes to the image, so you must verify the adjusted areas blend naturally with the rest of the photo.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative judgment of deciding if the targeted edits perfectly balance the specific area against the overall composition.
questions.check: Which areas does the selective tool show selected, and what values are about to apply?
questions.say_example: The selective tool targets <the shoreline> with saturation about to go to <+25>.

questions.question: Are the colour changes done and ready to apply?
questions.why: Clicking OK commits all the current Camera Raw edits to the image layer in the main Photoshop workspace.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the final subjective review of the color and tone adjustments before they are baked into the image.
questions.verify_form: The agent committed the Camera Raw edits with OK - check the final review.
questions.check: What Camera Raw values are shown about to commit with OK?
questions.say_example: Camera Raw is about to apply with <white balance and exposure changes only>.

questions.question: Are you ready to tap 'Done' and save your edits?
questions.why: The yellow 'Done' button commits your final adjustments to the image, so you must be certain the editing process is complete.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the final subjective judgment of whether the edited photo meets your standards before saving the changes.
questions.verify_form: The agent tapped Done, or is about to - check the edit meets your standards first.
questions.check: Does the edit stack shown before tapping Done match what was discussed as the finished look?
questions.say_example: Before tapping Done, the stack shows <the crop, color grade and vignette> all applied.

questions.question: Which extension or external app should you send this photo to?
questions.why: The share sheet displays various external apps like PS Express alongside built-in tools like Markup, requiring a choice on where to route the image next.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to choose the specific external tool or extension that best fits your intended final touches or export workflow.
questions.verify_form: The agent sent the photo to an extension or another app from the share sheet - check which one and that nothing was posted.
questions.check: Which app or extension does the page show selected in the share sheet?
questions.say_example: The share sheet shows <PS Express> selected.

questions.question: Is the JPEG being made through the Image Processor with the settings you wanted?
questions.why: Selecting the Image Processor from the Tools menu determines the specific workflow and settings used to generate the final output file.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to choose your preferred export utility and specific file conversion settings for the final image.
questions.verify_form: The agent converted the raw through the Image Processor - check the settings.
questions.check: What settings does the Image Processor dialog show for format, quality and destination?
questions.say_example: The Image Processor is set to <JPEG, quality 10, to a Processed folder>.

questions.question: Were the layers flattened the way you wanted before the save?
questions.why: The context menu displays multiple choices like 'Merge Visible' and 'Flatten Image' that determine exactly how the layer stack is consolidated.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to specify how the layers are merged and whether hidden layers are preserved or discarded before saving.
questions.verify_form: The agent flattened the layers before saving - check whether hidden layers were dropped and whether you wanted the layered file kept.
questions.check: Does the page show 'Merge Visible' or 'Flatten Image' chosen, and were any hidden layers dropped in the process?
questions.say_example: Flatten Image was chosen. <One hidden adjustment layer> gets dropped in the process.

questions.question: How do you want to save or share the finished image?
questions.why: The export menu offers distinct options for simply saving a copy, sharing to another app, or customizing the file's size and format.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses control over the final file's destination, format, and quality settings.
questions.verify_form: The agent chose Save, Share or Export - check which; Save writes a copy at the default size, Export is where size and format change.
questions.check: Which of Save, Share, or Export does the page show chosen?
questions.say_example: Export is the one chosen, opening the size and format settings.

questions.question: Which photo do you want to export?
questions.why: The screen displays a grid of several RAW photos in the album, requiring you to identify the exact image to use.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to choose the specific photograph from the album that will be exported.
questions.check: Which photo's thumbnail does the page show highlighted or selected in the grid?
questions.say_example: The grid shows <IMG_5521.CR2> highlighted. Export that one, or a different photo?

questions.question: Do you want to export the edited version or the unmodified original?
questions.why: The export menu offers a choice between exporting the edited photo or the unmodified original, determining whether your corrections are applied to the output file.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to choose whether to output the final corrected image or retrieve the raw, unedited original.
questions.check: Does the export menu show 'edited' or 'original' selected?
questions.say_example: Export is set to the original, unedited file, not your edited version. Keep it that way, or switch to the edited one?

questions.question: Will this export save a new copy, or overwrite the original?
questions.why: Overwriting the original RAW or high-res JPEG destroys the unedited baseline, preventing you from ever starting over or recovering the original data.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might permanently destroy the user's original photograph by saving over it, whereas a human would ensure a new file is generated.
questions.check: Does the export dialog indicate it will overwrite the original source file rather than save a new copy?
questions.say_example: This export would overwrite the original file in place. The unedited version won't be recoverable after. Go ahead, or save a copy instead?

questions.question: Quick export to the camera roll, or Export as, where the file type and watermark get set?
questions.why: The 'Export to Camera Roll' option quickly saves a default JPEG, while 'Export as...' provides crucial settings for choosing file formats, adjusting dimensions, and adding a personalized watermark.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to embed their copyright watermark or save the image in a higher-quality format for professional delivery.
questions.verify_form: The agent exported to the camera roll or used Export as - check which; only Export as sets the format, size and watermark.
questions.check: Does the page show a quick camera-roll export chosen when the ask asked for a specific size, format, or watermark?
questions.say_example: Camera Roll export was used, even though the ask called for <a specific export size>.

children.label: Set the format, quality, size and colour space

questions.question: Do you want to enable soft proofing to see how the colors will shift when printed?
questions.why: Checking the 'Soft Proofing' box simulates how the image's colors and contrast will change when printed on specific paper profiles, allowing you to make compensating corrections.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to anticipate and correct the inevitable dulling of colors that happens when moving from a backlit screen to a physical print.
questions.verify_form: The agent enabled soft proofing, or not - check whether you print.
questions.check: Is the Soft Proofing checkbox checked or unchecked?
questions.say_example: Left Soft Proofing <unchecked>

questions.question: Which file format should you choose to preserve your edits?
questions.why: Selecting a format like PSD ensures that all layers and non-destructive adjustments visible in the workspace remain intact for future editing.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to dictate the specific archival format needed to maintain your preferred editing workflow.
questions.verify_form: The agent chose a file format - check it preserves layers if you wanted them.
questions.check: Which file format does the export dialog show selected?
questions.say_example: The export is set to save as <JPEG>, which won't keep the layers.

questions.question: Are the format, quality and folder right to export with?
questions.why: Checking the JPEG quality, color profile, and destination folder ensures the final image is exported correctly for its intended use.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally balance file size against image quality and verify your specific copyright metadata is embedded.
questions.verify_form: The agent set the export's format, quality and location - check each field; JPEG at High to a folder you know is the usual answer.
questions.check: What do the format, quality and destination fields show on the export dialog before confirming?
questions.say_example: Set to export as <JPEG, quality 100, to ~/Exports>. Go ahead and export?

questions.question: Are your export settings correct, and are you exporting the intended number of images?
questions.why: Confirming the export parameters and file count ensures the final image is saved in the correct format and size without accidentally exporting unintended files.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the final opportunity to verify the output resolution, format, and exact file selection before the image is written to your drive.
questions.verify_form: The agent set the export settings and the number of images - check format, size and that the count matches the frames you edited.
questions.check: Do the export settings and the image count shown on the dialog match what was intended?
questions.say_example: Exporting <6 images> at <JPEG, quality 90>. Does that match what you wanted?

questions.question: Do you want to apply a watermark to protect your exported image?
questions.why: The export dialog contains a watermark checkbox and settings, which are necessary to protect the image from unauthorized use and to brand it when shared online.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to protect their intellectual property and brand the image before it leaves their control.
questions.verify_form: The agent added a watermark or left it off - check which; a watermark on a file for a client is usually wrong, on a public post usually wanted.
questions.check: Is the watermark checkbox on, and is the stated destination a client delivery or a public post?
questions.say_example: The watermark is turned <on> for what's described as <a client delivery>. Clients usually get clean files.

questions.question: Is the export colour space sRGB, so it looks right on phones and browsers?
questions.why: Exporting in Adobe RGB or ProPhoto RGB for web use will cause the image to look washed out and dull on most unmanaged displays.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might preserve the wide editing color space for the final export, resulting in a photo that looks terrible when the user shares it online.
questions.check: What color space does the export dialog show selected - sRGB, Adobe RGB, or ProPhoto RGB?
questions.say_example: The export is set to <Adobe RGB>, which can look washed out and dull on standard displays.

questions.question: Is the export's file size under the limit of where it's going?
questions.why: Exporting a 100% quality, full-resolution JPEG might result in a 30MB file that fails to upload to social media or email, requiring you to limit the file size or resolution in the export settings.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might generate a file that the user ultimately cannot use for their intended purpose without going back and re-exporting.
questions.check: What estimated file size does the export dialog show, and what platform is named as the destination?
questions.say_example: The estimated size reads <32MB>, heading to <an email attachment>, which usually caps around 25MB.

questions.question: Which export recipe should you select to format the output images?
questions.why: Capture One uses pre-configured export recipes that bundle file format, resolution, and output location into a single checkbox, allowing for simultaneous exports to different specifications.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the efficiency and precision of utilizing predefined recipes tailored to their specific delivery requirements, risking incorrect file formats or sizes.
questions.verify_form: The agent picked an export recipe - check its format, resolution and destination folder.
questions.check: Which export recipe name does the page show checked, and what format, resolution and destination does it bundle?
questions.say_example: The <Web JPEG> recipe is checked, bundling <JPEG, 2048px, to a Web Exports folder>.

children.label: Set the metadata and the file name

questions.question: Do you want to strip location metadata from the exported photo for privacy?
questions.why: The export dialog often includes options to embed or remove location info, which is a critical privacy decision if the photo was taken at a private residence and is being posted publicly.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses control over their personal privacy and safety if the agent exports the file with GPS coordinates still attached.
questions.verify_form: The agent stripped or kept location metadata - check for privacy.
questions.check: Is the metadata-strip or remove-location-info checkbox checked?
questions.say_example: Location metadata is left <in>, on a photo described as <a home interior>, heading to <a public post>.

questions.question: Where do you want to save the exported photograph?
questions.why: The export dialog displays specific organizational folders like '01 Projects' and '02 Areas', so selecting the correct destination ensures the file fits into your existing storage system.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means the agent might save the file to a generic location like the Desktop rather than organizing it properly into your specific project folders.
questions.verify_form: The agent chose a save destination - check the folder.
questions.check: Which destination folder does the page show selected?
questions.say_example: The destination folder shows <02 Areas>.

questions.question: Is the export warning that a file with this name already exists there?
questions.why: Overwriting an existing file is a destructive action, requiring the user to decide whether to replace the old file or rename the new export to save both.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to prevent the accidental deletion of a previous version or original file by renaming the current export.
questions.check: Does the export dialog show a warning that a file with this name already exists at the destination?
questions.say_example: The dialog warns a file named <IMG_5521.jpg> already exists at the destination.

questions.question: Does a save dialog actually appear and finish for the PSD, or is the save only talked about?
questions.why: The narrator states the file is being saved as a PSD, but the screen never displays the save dialog or the final file being written out.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent relying on this demonstration misses the critical UI steps required to configure and confirm the final export.
questions.check: Does the page ever show a save dialog and completion for the PSD file, after the narration states it is being saved?
questions.say_example: The narration says it's saving as PSD, but no save dialog or completion ever appears on screen.

questions.question: Did the Image Processor successfully create the new JPEG folder in the expected location?
questions.why: Seeing the new 'JPEG' folder appear next to the original raw file confirms that the export process executed correctly and routed the files to the right destination.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the immediate visual confirmation that your exported files are organized exactly where you need them for the next step in your workflow.
questions.check: Does a new JPEG folder appear next to the original raw file after the Image Processor runs?
questions.say_example: New JPEG folder appeared next to <the raw file>

questions.question: Does the number of images you are exporting match the number you originally imported?
questions.why: Checking that the 'Export 6 Images' button matches the initial 'Import 6 Images' count ensures no photos were accidentally skipped during the editing session.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance of personally verifying that the entire batch of photos was successfully processed without any omissions.
questions.check: Does the 'Export N Images' button's count match the 'Import N Images' count shown earlier?
questions.say_example: Import showed <6 Images>, but Export now reads <5 Images>.

questions.question: Is the exported file actually in the destination folder, or did the export fail quietly?
questions.why: Exporting high-res images can fail silently in the background if the drive is full or permissions are wrong, leaving you without the final file even if the dialog closed normally.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might close the application assuming the task is done, losing all the work because the final file was never written to disk.
questions.check: Does the destination folder show the exported file present, or does the page show any disk space or permission error?
questions.say_example: No error shows, but the destination folder doesn't yet show <the exported file>.

questions.question: Did the export progress bar finish, or stall or show an error?
questions.why: High-resolution exports take time, and the editor displays a progress bar in the corner that vanishes upon success but will hang or flag an error if the render fails.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user cannot visually confirm that the file was actually written to the disk successfully rather than failing silently in the background.
questions.check: Does the background export progress indicator show completion, an error icon, or does it stay stuck?
questions.say_example: The progress indicator has been stuck at <60%> without moving.

questions.question: Did the colors shift unexpectedly in the final exported file?
questions.why: Exporting an image edited in a wide color space like ProPhoto RGB down to sRGB for web use can cause a visible loss of saturation or color shifts, requiring a final visual check of the actual output file.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the final visual quality control check, risking an agent blindly delivering an exported file that looks duller or noticeably different than the master edit you approved.
questions.check: Does the exported file's color space differ from the working space, and does opening it show a visible saturation shift?
questions.say_example: The export went from <ProPhoto RGB> down to <sRGB>, and the opened file looks less saturated than the editor's preview.

children.label: Carry the edit to other photos
children.note: 9.8.1 or 9.8.2 to capture the edit - 9.8.2 if the settings need to be saved for another session. then the person applies them to the next photo in 9.8.3 and checks how they look in 8.1. OSj7 does 9.8.1 mid-session between two photos; OXgO's style includes all the editing settings used for the shoot.

questions.question: Do the copied settings suit this photo's own light, or is it a blind paste?
questions.why: The three-dot menu reveals the 'Paste Settings' option required to instantly transfer previously copied edits onto the current photo.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to decide if the pasted batch of settings actually suits the unique lighting and composition of this specific photo.
questions.verify_form: The agent pasted another image's settings onto this photo - check the look suits this photo's light; a preset paste is not a correction.
questions.check: After the paste, does the preview show the pasted settings pushing this photo into clipping or a colour cast that the source photo didn't have?
questions.say_example: This photo's own light is different from the one the settings were copied from. Paste anyway, or build fresh settings for this one?

questions.question: Should you manually adjust the tone curve or copy settings from a previous edit?
questions.why: The screen shows the option to copy settings from a previous photo in the filmstrip, which ensures a consistent cinematic look without manually rebuilding the curve.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative judgment of deciding whether this specific photo needs a custom tone curve or if a previously established cinematic look should be reused.
questions.verify_form: The agent copied the previous photo's curve or built a new one - check which; a copied curve may not suit this light.
questions.check: Does the page show a manual tone curve built, or settings copied from a previous photo in the filmstrip?
questions.say_example: Settings were copied from <the previous photo> rather than building a new curve for this one's light.

questions.question: Which specific develop settings do you want to copy to the clipboard?
questions.why: The dialog presents checkboxes for every adjustment category, requiring a deliberate choice about which edits are universally applicable versus specific to this single image.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to selectively exclude image-specific adjustments, risking an agent blindly pasting inappropriate edits like local masks or crops onto other photos.
questions.verify_form: The agent chose which settings to copy - check masks and crop were excluded unless you wanted them on other photos.
questions.check: Which checkboxes are checked in the Copy Settings dialog - are Masks and Crop included?
questions.say_example: Masks and Crop are <checked> in the Copy Settings dialog, so they'll carry to the other photos too.

questions.question: Were the develop settings copied for the other photos?
questions.why: The context menu reveals a 'Develop Settings' sub-menu where you can select 'Copy Settings...' to duplicate your current edits.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to manually capture your finalized edit settings to efficiently process other similar photos in a batch.
questions.check: Does the context menu show 'Copy Settings...' was used, and does the paste target show updated thumbnails?
questions.say_example: Pasted the settings onto <4 other photos in the filmstrip>

questions.question: Do the masks listed in the Copy Settings dialog match the local adjustments you created earlier?
questions.why: Verifying that the dialog lists Mask 3, Mask 2, and Mask 1 confirms that the Subject, Object, and Brush masks created earlier were properly registered by the software.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the peace of mind that comes from manually confirming their complex local adjustments are actually included before copying settings.
questions.check: Does the Copy Settings dialog list every mask created earlier in this session, one entry per mask?
questions.say_example: The dialog lists <Mask 1 and Mask 2> only. <The third brush mask> made earlier isn't there.

questions.question: What do you want to call this preset, and what should go in it?
questions.why: The 'New Develop Preset' dialog requires a custom name and specific checkbox selections to determine exactly which current adjustments are saved for future use.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to establish their own naming conventions and curate exactly which edits are saved into their personal preset library.
questions.verify_form: The agent named the preset and chose its settings - check the name is one you will find again and that masks and crop are excluded.
questions.check: What name does the page show for the new preset, and which checkboxes are checked for included settings?
questions.say_example: The preset is named <Warm Portrait>, with Masks and Crop left unchecked.

questions.question: Is the Optics box checked, so the lens corrections go into the preset?
questions.why: The screen showed lens corrections enabled in the Optics tab, but the Optics checkbox was left unchecked during preset creation, meaning those specific corrections will not be saved.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the automatic application of chromatic aberration removal and lens corrections when applying this preset to future photos.
questions.check: Is the Optics checkbox checked in the preset dialog, given lens corrections were enabled in the Optics tab?
questions.say_example: The Optics tab has lens corrections on, but the Optics box in the preset dialog is left unchecked.

questions.question: Should the Geometry box be checked, since rotation or aspect changed?
questions.why: The screen shows you made specific rotation and aspect changes, but leaving the Geometry box unchecked means those edits will not be saved in the preset.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to reuse their carefully tuned perspective and rotation fixes because the agent failed to include them in the saved preset.
questions.verify_form: The agent left Geometry unchecked in the preset - check whether you wanted it saved.
questions.check: Is the Geometry checkbox unchecked in the preset dialog, given rotation or aspect changes were made?
questions.say_example: Rotation and aspect were changed, but the Geometry box in the preset dialog is left unchecked.

children.label: Apply it to the next photo and judge the fit

questions.question: With the style on, does any thumbnail look off next to the others?
questions.why: Previewing the style across different browser thumbnails confirms whether the Smart Adjustments successfully normalize exposure and white balance for varying shots.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to visually verify that the automated style adjustments maintain your desired aesthetic across diverse lighting scenarios.
questions.check: With the style applied, does any thumbnail look overexposed, undersaturated or off next to the others?
questions.say_example: Previewed across <five thumbnails>, one shot in different light comes out <noticeably overexposed>.
